profile.summary: Isaiah is a prophetic book that responds, with a strong tone of judgment and hope, to the question whether God can save his people from the powers of the world, from sin and from its consequences. The introduction presents it as a work that confronts unbelief, denounces idolatry and calls for exclusive trust in the Lord. The prophet begins his ministry with a vision of God's holiness, greatness and love, and this experience shapes the whole book: God is absolutely reliable, judges sin, but also preserves a remnant and promises restoration by his grace. For a Christian reader, the book points to Christ's coming as the true Emmanuel and the just King who brings together a new people.
profile.setting: The main backdrop is the southern kingdom, Judah, between the death of King Uzziah (740 BC) and the post-exile. The period is marked by the aggressive expansion of Assyria, which threatens Israel, Judah, and other nations of the region. Judah oscillates between political covenants and dependence on God: Ahaz turns to Assyria and suffers the consequences; Hezekiah trusts in the Lord and is delivered in 701 BC. Then comes the threat and Babylonian exile (605-586 BC), followed by the return of a remnant in 538 BC. The literary environment of the book brings together discourses of judgment, regrets, parables, judicial processes, promises of salvation, hymns, oracles against nations, Messiah's announcements, songs of the servant and historical narratives. The traditional authorship is attributed to Isaiah, but the introduction recognizes that many scholars question whether the whole book came from his hand, since it deals with three distinct historical moments; yet, the literary unity and the use that Jesus and the New Testament make of the book support the reading of an Iayan work.

structure.label: Early Confrontation with the Sin of Judah
structure.description: It portrays the present corruption of Judah in contrast to the original call to life in the presence of God, exposing the need for purification and return to the Lord.

structure.label: Called the Prophet and Crisis of Trust
structure.description: Isaiah's vision and the episodes linked to Ahaz's time show that renewal begins with repentance and trust in God, not human covenants.

structure.label: Judgment, nations and the only secure trust
structure.description: Varied messages and literary forms reinforce that the Lord is the only trustworthy, and that relying on neighboring nations or any created power is foolishness.

structure.label: Rescue under Hezekiah and final warning
structure.description: The historical narratives show the deliverance before Assyria when there is confidence in God, but also the human fragility that anticipates future exile.

structure.label: Comfort in the exile and superiority of God
structure.description: He speaks to the exiles in Babylon, stating that the Lord has not been overcome and is infinitely superior to idols and oppressive powers.

structure.label: Restoration by God's Graceful Action
structure.description: Respond to the deepest problem: the sin of the people. God promises to rescue a remnant and accomplish this through the suffering of his Servant.

structure.label: Holy life of the restored and new people
structure.description: After the return, the book calls for purity, justice and exclusive devotion, describing the formation of a renewed community under the rule of the Lord and his righteous king.

themes: The holiness of God and his majesty above all else
Exclusive trust in the Lord instead of covenants, human power or idols
Judgment for sin and hope of restoration
The Messiah, the suffering Servant and the new community of God's people
readingKeys: Notice how each historical bloc responds to a concrete crisis: Assyria, exile and post-exile.
Always compare judgment and hope: Isaiah denounces sin, but also shows the way of restoration.
Notice the insistence on trust, holiness and exclusivity of devotion; the book deals with both politics and heart.
profile.cautions: The introduction recognizes debate about authorship and date: many scholars question whether the prophet Isaiah wrote the whole book, but the proposed reading affirms literary unity and possibility of prophetic proclamation of the future. When reading, avoid artificially separating judgment and hope: the book keeps both united. Nor does it reduce Isaiah to isolated predictions; it presents a broad view of God, human sin, exile and the final restoration of his people.

dossier.narratedEra: The book tells of the crisis of Judah from the end of Uzziah's reign (740 BC) to the post-exile, focusing on three great historical moments: the Assyrian threat in the 8th century BC, Babylonian exile and restoration after 538/539 BC. The main setting of Isaiah 1-39 is Judah from the period of Uzziah, Ahaz and Hezekiah, with Assyria advancing against the nations of the Mediterranean coast; Isaiah 40-55 projects the situation of exile; and Isaiah 56-66 deals with the life of the people already back to the earth. The composition, however, is presented by the notes as a process over time: materials of 6-39 would have been recorded at various times between about 740 and 701 BC, and 40-66 probably came after 701 BC, perhaps with an interval of more than fifteen years between these blocks.
dossier.compositionEra: The tradition presented in the notes attributes the book to the prophet Isaiah, consistently called as author of the set, with the possibility of having been recorded prophecies at different times of his ministerial life. Tyndale's introduction notes that many modern scholars have gone on to defend multiple authorship since the mid-19th century, because the book addresses three distinct historical situations, including two beyond the life of the prophet; but the same source states that divine inspiration allows predictive prophecy and supports the literary unity of the book. Matthew Henry also places Isaiah among the prophets writers and places him in the final period of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, with the beginning sometime after the prophets Hosea, Joel, Amos, and Obadiah. Notes do not offer a unique final writing date, only a layered composition throughout the ministry and possibly beyond it.

politics.title: Rise of Assyria as dominant power
politics.detail: Assyria, after about fifty years of relative quietness, re-increased around 740 BC and advances from the territory of present-day northern Iraq to the southwest, towards Egypt. On the way, it subdues small nations of the Mediterranean coast, including Israel and Judah. The notes indicate that Assyria had already taken Galilee and much of the Israeli territory east of the Jordan, and that it was not content with partial control, but wanted total domination over Israel, Judah and the other small peoples of the region.
politics.readingImpact: This background makes prophecies against political trust a concrete critique: the temptation to seek security in neighboring empires appears as spiritual follies, not just diplomatic error.

politics.title: Reign of Uzziah and the succession crisis in Judah
politics.detail: As Uzias lived, Judah was able to ignore the international crisis; the notes describe him as a good and effective king, with a strong army. After his death, however, he succeeded him ungodly rulers, and in this vacuum of leadership Isaiah receives the vision that inaugurates his ministry. Matthew Henry places the prophet in the environment of the end of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, and Tyndale associates the beginning of the ministry with the year of Uzziah's death.
politics.readingImpact: The death of Uzziah changes the reading of Isaiah's call: the prophet arises exactly when political stability and human trust fail, highlighting God's holiness and reliability as the only sure basis.

politics.title: Syro-Ephraimite Coalition and the policy of Ahaz
politics.detail: By 734 BC, Israel and Syria form a coalition against Assyria. As Ahaz of Judah refuses to join, these two kingdoms attack Judah to force him into the covenant. Instead of trusting in God, Ahaz calls the Assyrians to his help. Assyria defeats Syria and Israel, but also subdues Judah and imposes heavy tribute.
politics.readingImpact: This episode explains why Isaiah insists that trusting foreign powers produces submission and burden, not salvation; the reading of Is 7 gains character of confrontation with a real political and theological choice.

politics.title: Fall of the Northern Kingdom
politics.detail: The notes record that Assyria again defeated the kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and took most of the people into exile. Tyndale also notes, in 1:1, that the reference to Samaria and Ephraim points to the north and to the fall of Israel.
politics.readingImpact: The fall of Israel functions as a historical warning for Judah: the judgment announced is not hypothetical, but has already happened to a brother kingdom.

politics.title: Senaqueribe campaign against Judah
politics.detail: In 701 BC, during the reign of Hezekiah, Assyria again invaded Judah. The notes present this moment as a decisive contrast: Judah now depends on the faithfulness of God, and the Lord redeems the nation from the Assyrian hand. In Isaiah 33, the destruction of cities around Jerusalem and the terror caused by the Assyrian officials reinforce this scenario.
politics.readingImpact: The reader understands chapters 36-39 and certain images of 33 as narratives of real military threat; salvation is not abstract, but historical deliverance of siege and intimidation.

politics.title: Babylonian exile and subsequent restoration
politics.detail: The notes date the Babylonian domination over Judah between 605 and 586 BC, followed by a return in 538/539 BC. Isaiah 40-55 responds to the problem of exile, and 56-66 to the temptations of the people after the return. The restoration is attributed to the grace of God, not to the faithfulness of the remnant.
politics.readingImpact: This broadens the reading of the book beyond the Assyrian crisis: the same God who judges also preserves a remnant and prepares the return, which structures the hope of the final chapters.

customs.title: sacrificial worship without obedience
customs.detail: Is 1:11-15 is read as a denunciation of sacrifices, incense, godly meetings, fasts, and feasts which God no longer accepts because of the moral corruption of the people. The notes point out that the Lord wants Judah to stop with religious exercises done in a hypocritical way, not just to continue them. The incense should be a pleasant aroma, but in the context of hypocrisy, it becomes a disgusting odor.
customs.readingImpact: The worship in the temple cannot be read as an automatic guarantee of divine favor; ethical holiness conditions the value of the ritual.

customs.title: Festive days, new moon and religious calendar
customs.detail: The notes mention the celebrations of the new moon, with sacrifices, meals and rest of the work, in addition to the great annual festivals: Easter, Harvest, Trumpets and Cabanas/Tabernaculars. These elements appear in Is 1:13-14 as part of the institutional cult of Judah.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that Isaiah criticizes not the existence of a sacred calendar, but his practice unlinked from justice and fidelity.

customs.title: Urban life and vulnerability of Jerusalem
customs.detail: Jerusalem is presented as the daughter of Zion, an image linked to the protective presence of God; but in Ih 1:8 it appears as a weakened city, as a shelter abandoned under siege. In 33:17-24, the vision of Zion includes the king, the land without apparent borders, and the community of the people of God.
customs.readingImpact: The holy city ceases to be an automatic symbol of security and is now assessed by the fidelity of the people and by the real presence of God.

customs.title: Social structure marked by injustice
customs.detail: Is 1:10 and 1:17 presuppose "leaders" and "people" at all social levels, and corruption includes oppression of orphans and widows, as well as innocent victims. Justice is defined as the protection of the weak and marginalized. The notes also draw attention to the metaphor of Jerusalem as a whore, an image of infidelity.
customs.readingImpact: National sin in Isaiah is not only false cult, but a perverted social order; this guides the ethical reading of the book to its full extent.

customs.title: Agricultural Paganism and Religiosity of the Woods
customs.detail: The notes of Is 1:29-30 describe the practice of idolatry in oak groves and gardens dedicated to idols, linked to the Canaanite religion of Baal. These places were seen as bearers of blessing, but Isaiah treats them as a source of spiritual death.
customs.readingImpact: The condemnation not only targets carved images, but religious practices linked to fertility and false agricultural security.

customs.title: Tribute and imperial domination
customs.detail: Judah's submission to Assyria after Ahaz's request includes a heavy burden of taxation. In 33:1, the notes also observe that wicked nations break political agreements when this suits them.
customs.readingImpact: The reader understands that international alliances in Isaiah have material and moral cost; foreign policy is part of the drama of faith.

language.title: Vision as a unit key of the book
language.detail: In 1:1, "visions" introduces the book as a unified whole and covers the ministry of Isaiah for about fifty-five years, from about 740 to 685 BC. The term is not only treated as private experience, but as an editorial frame for the set.
language.readingImpact: The opening guides the reading of the whole book as a coherent prophetic vision, not as a loose collection of oracles.

language.title: The Holy One of Israel as a recurring title
language.detail: The notes of 1:4 highlight the Holy One of Israel as a frequent and theologically dense title: God is a just, incomparable and redeeming king. In 1:24, the same God, usually protector, appears as the one who disciplines the people themselves.
language.readingImpact: The epithet reinforces that Judah's problem is not the absence of God, but rejection of the holy God who has already revealed himself to them.

language.title: Meat of injured body and national disease
language.detail: In 1:5-6, the nation is described as a beaten body, with a wounded head, sick heart and without treatment. The notes connect the image to the Assyrian attack and the spiritual definition of the people.
language.readingImpact: The body figure makes the reader feel the gravity of the rebellion: the damage is social, political and spiritual at the same time.

language.title: Purification by whiteness, washing and refining
language.detail: In 1:16-18, the vocabulary of washing, cleaning, scarlet, crimson, snow and wool indicates radical transformation and purification. In 1:25-27, the image of casting and removal of impurities shows that exile serves to refine the people.
language.readingImpact: Language does not describe mere moral improvement, but a recreation of the community by divine action.

language.title: Zion as remnant and restored community
language.detail: The notes note that in 1:27 "Sião" refers to the remaining community, and in 33:17-24 the vision of government in Zion involves the king as the human representative of the Great King. In 66:18-23, nations can even serve as priests and Levites before God.
language.readingImpact: It ceases to be only geographical location and becomes an image of people purified, governed by God and open to the nations.

language.title: cosmic images of throne, temple and fire
language.detail: In 66:1-2, God states that heaven is his throne and the earth his footer, relativizing any temple as the limit of his presence. In 66:6, the noise of the temple and vengeance against the rebels echo scenes of judgment; in 66:15-16, God comes with fire to judge. The notes also connect 66:1-2 to Stephen's speech in Acts 7.
language.readingImpact: Language broadens the horizon of the book: God does not fit in a building and his judgment/redenation reaches all creation.

timeline.title: 740 BC - death of Uzziah and the beginning of visionary ministry
timeline.detail: The notes place the historical starting point of the book in Uzziah's death, around 740 BC, when the Assyrian crisis intensifies and Isaiah receives the vision that casts his ministry.
timeline.readingImpact: The opening of the book gains historical weight: Isaiah speaks in a moment of transition and instability, not in quiet times.

timeline.title: c. 734 BC - Syro-Ephraimite war
timeline.detail: Israel and Syria form a front against Assyria and attack Judah to coerce Ahaz to join the coalition. Ahaz asks Assyria for help instead of trusting in God.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone clarifies the immediate background of Is 7 and shows how the political crisis has become a crisis of faith.

timeline.title: 722 BC. O fall of Israel to Assyria
timeline.detail: Assyria defeats the northern kingdom and exiles most of its population. Tyndale also relates this reality to the oracles against Samaria/Ephraim.
timeline.readingImpact: The destruction of Israel confirms the pattern of judgment announced in Isaiah and acts as a warning for Judah.

timeline.title: 701 BC O Assyrian invasion of Judah and deliverance in Jerusalem
timeline.detail: During the reign of Hezekiah, Senaquerrib invades Judah. The notes describe devastated cities, unknown Assyrian language, and the terror of the officers, but also the ransom of God in Jerusalem.
timeline.readingImpact: Chapters 36-39 and certain images of 33 should be read as a testimony of concrete historical deliverance, not just spiritual metaphor.

timeline.title: 605'586 BC - Fall of Judah and Babylonian exile
timeline.detail: The notes summarize the period when Judah is won by Babylon, after Assyria. This stage answers the questions raised by Isaiah about the reliability of God before the national ruin.
timeline.readingImpact: Chapters 40-55 are read as a prophetic response to the experience of exile, apparent defeat and the need for restoration.

timeline.title: 538/539 BC - Return of exile
timeline.detail: The return is associated with 538 BC in Tyndale and 539 BC in the introductory summary, showing historical rapprochement between the fall of Babylon and the restoration of the people. The return is attributed to the gracious action of God.
timeline.readingImpact: Chapters 56-66 are now read as an exhortation to a restored people, but still in danger of repeating ancient corruption.

investigation: Tyndale's introduction is more explicit about the general historical frame than about internal details of each textual block; therefore, the compositional chronology is presented in probable, unclosed terms.

Matthew Henry offers a devotional and confessional view of the history of the prophets, including traditions about the family of Isaiah and their proximity to the court, but this information does not appear as historical data proven in Tyndale's notes.
The given notes are strongly concentrated in Isaiah 1, 33 and 66; the intermediate chapters are cited only selectively, especially to support the general structure of the book.

There is a tension point on the date of the return of exile: the introduction mentions 538 BC, while the abstract mentions 539 BC; the source does not solve this difference, so it was marked as debated.

The readings of unique authorship and literary unity are presented in a confessional and textual way, while the multi-layered academic hypothesis is mentioned only as a majority current since the nineteenth century.

The notes cite several New Testament texts as echoes or quotations from Isaiah, but here they were used only when they served the literary or theological characterization explicitly mentioned in the sources.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the attached notes and therefore covers only the contexts, customs, language and historical landmarks that they explicitly discuss. No external data on chronology, politics, institutions, archaeology or authorship have been added. The cover is selective: there is strong detailing Isaiah 1, 33 and 66, and less direct information about other sections. Some dates appear in an approximate or small variation between sources; in these cases, I preferred to indicate uncertainty rather than harmonization on their own. I also kept separate the historical setting of the book and the proposals on when the text was written, as requested, without confusing narrated scenario with date of composition.
